item.title: Could Your Child's Anxiety Actually Be This?
item.description:
PANDAS

Could Your Child's Anxiety Actually Be This?

When a sudden change in your child's mood is a message from their immune system.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Real overthinking creeps, but this kind flips a switch.
  • The “switch” that's more easily overlooked is in the immune system, not the mind.
  • A strep infection or another illness can trigger the immune system to attack the brain.

Most of the time, I see overthinking in children build slowly. It's a worry here, a reassurance-seeking habit there, until a child is quietly stuck in a loop. But every so often in my more than 35 years as a child psychologist, a parent describes something stranger: Their easygoing kid becomes, almost overnight, someone unrecognizable. Parents say things like "He is obsessed with needing reassurance," or "All of a sudden she's terrified of germs or mistakes." The theme is kids who suddenly panic over things that never bothered them a week earlier. That’s not typical overthinking. That’s a red flag.

Real Overthinking Creeps; This Kind Flips a Switch

Ordinary overthinking develops like a spider spinning a web. By this metaphor, I mean one worry connects to the next until a child is quietly tangled. It has a history you can trace: a hard year, a sensitive temperament, a perfectionistic streak. What I’m describing in the current article has no history. Parents use the same word every time: overnight. One week their child is fine; the next, they’re consumed by obsessive worry, new tics, or meltdowns that don’t fit their personality.

Sometimes the “Switch” Is in the Immune System, Not the Mind

In a small number of cases, this sudden flip isn’t rooted in psychology at all—it’s rooted in the immune system. PANDAS (pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections) and PANS (pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome) are conditions in which a strep infection or another illness triggers the immune system to mistakenly attack the brain, producing sudden obsessive thoughts, extreme anxiety, tics, or food restriction almost overnight. I'm especially grateful to have someone in my personal circle—my wife, a physician who specialized in PANDAS and PANS before her recent retirement—who first helped alert me to how often this connection gets missed.

Know When to Look Past Psychology

I share the case of Austin (fictitious name), age 10, in my new book, When Overthinking Takes Over Your Child: 10 Days to Ease Anxiety, Quiet Worry, and Tame Runaway Thoughts—a boy whose sudden reassurance-seeking and fear that everyone was mad at him traced back to a recent strep infection, not a personality change.

Austin’s pediatrician wasn’t initially concerned; his teachers were baffled. It took a specialist connecting his sudden symptoms to that recent strep infection before antibiotics and anti-inflammatory treatment brought him back to himself within two weeks. If your child’s overthinking arrives suddenly, alongside handwriting regression, new tics, or drastic mood swings, that timeline matters more than any worksheet or calming script. It’s worth a conversation with a pediatric neurologist or PANDAS/PANS specialist before assuming you’re dealing with ordinary anxiety.

The Takeaway

Most overthinking is exactly what it looks like: a worried mind that needs coaching, not medicine. But every parent deserves to know that occasionally, the switch really did just flip—and the fastest path back to their child isn’t a mindset shift. It’s a proper medical diagnosis.

item.title: Vaping Is an Addiction
item.description:
Vaping

Vaping Is an Addiction

Addressing vaping in our families, schools, and communities, and in our own lives.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Vaping creates and maintains real nicotine dependence by hijacking the brain's reward system.
  • Whether e-cigarettes are uniquely addictive compared to cigarettes is a question still being researched.
  • Communities and schools have a role in preventing youth dependency.

Public opinion shifts quickly in our post-digital era. E-cigarettes were only available in the United States for about eight years before they started to fall out of favor. As of 2014, more than half of Americans consider vaping at least as harmful as smoking (Malt et al., 2020). Compared to the roughly six decades before cigarettes crossed the 50-percent harm-awareness threshold, that’s lightning fast.

However, there is still work to do. About 7.2 million Americans believe vaping is harmless, and 57 million more believe it’s less harmful than smoking. The truth is, we don’t know every aspect of how harmful aerosolized nicotine is compared to freebase nicotine. But we do know it isn’t harmless.

Despite a shifting public opinion, we continue to see the portion of American adults who vape increasing year over year (Vahratian et al., 2025). Many try to quit (Rosen & Steinberg, 2019), some succeed (Sakhuja et al., 2025), and many more intend to quit (Palmer et al., 2023).

What Is Stopping E-Cigarette Users From Quitting?

We already know nicotine is addictive. When a person consumes nicotine in any form, it binds to the body’s nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, stimulating dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. This region of the brain is our reward system’s “boss,” and that dopamine release drives reinforcement, eventually leading to dependency if consumption is repeated over time.

Unique Addictive Properties?

But researchers think there may be something special about the addiction potential of aerosolized nicotine salts as a delivery mechanism. A 2019 study found that e-cigarette users and dual users had higher nicotine dependency scores compared to those of smokers (Jankowski et al., 2019).

Another study, which found that vaping triggered greater nucleus accumbens activation than smoking, concluded that this could, in fact, make e-cigarettes an effective smoking cessation method, potentially “rewarding” users away from smoking (Grundinger et al., 2025). This harm-reduction approach may be valid in theory, but when nearly all of the products available in the United States are smuggled, we can’t be sure we aren’t simply trading one set of harms for another.

Withdrawal

The nature of addiction is such that users often continue long after they stop wanting to, because withdrawal is physically, emotionally, and mentally torturous. Nicotine withdrawal is known to bring:

  • Intense cravings
  • Irritability
  • Brain fog
  • Mental health changes
  • Sleep disruption
  • Headaches
  • Dizziness
  • Digestive disruption
  • Respiratory symptoms

It’s all temporary, but the discomfort is very hard for people to sit with when they know exactly what will put a quick stop to it. In that moment, the substance seems like medicine rather than the poison it has been.

Is e-cigarette withdrawal any worse than withdrawing from other nicotine products? Paradoxically, it seems not. In fact, one study found that people quitting e-cigarettes reported fewer withdrawal symptoms than those quitting conventional cigarettes (Hughes et al., 2019). This brings us briefly back to the idea of harm reduction. With appropriate regulation and a better understanding of its health impacts, a product that is more appealing to the brain chemistry than cigarettes but easier to quit may have benefits.

Intervention and Quitting

The U.S. Public Health Service recommends that primary care physicians ask patients at every visit about tobacco use as part of a “five A’s” approach (Okuyemi et al., 2006):

  • Ask about tobacco use.
  • Advise on behavior modification.
  • Assess severity and the patient’s disposition toward quitting.
  • Assist with resources, referrals, prescriptions as needed, or a plan to quit.
  • Arrange a follow-up, check-in, or labs as needed.

Additionally, several screening methods fit into the Assess step. The ones most widely used in the United States are the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND) for adults and CRAFFT screening for adolescents.

Limited research indicates that of those who attempt to quit vaping, about a quarter are successful (Bejarano et al., 2024). Many methods and combinations are available to those wishing to stop, but the top choices according to the research are as follows:

  • Most effective stand-alone methods: Varenicline (Chantix), cytisinicline (used widely in Europe and expected to receive U.S. Food and Drug Administration [FDA] approval in 2027; Livingstone‐Banks et al., 2024).
  • Most effective approach overall: A combination of medication—specifically nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) or bupropion—and behavioral therapy (Guillaumier et al., 2023; Glover et al., 2003; Glover & Glover, 2001).

How Can Families Help?

Nicotine dependency is very much a physical phenomenon that often requires medication, but environmental and emotional factors matter, at least to those attempting to quit. Research finds little to no statistical difference in cessation success resulting from strong family support, but a 2017 study of smokers found individual preferences in three main categories:

  • Practical support: Helping pay for NRT or medication, assistance with environmental changes, such as removing triggers.
  • Emotional encouragement: Verbal praise or encouragement, calls or texts, compassion and grace around withdrawal and relapse, gentle reminders about goals and purpose.
  • Behavior modification: Not using nicotine in their presence, not inviting them to places that might be triggering.

Youth Use and Dependency

Nicotine and e-cigarette devices themselves appear to be particularly harmful to adolescents and young adults. Parents have their role in supporting prevention or cessation, which we’ve covered elsewhere. But there is vast opportunity at the school and community levels, too.

Community Interventions

Perhaps the best thing communities can do is reduce youth access. State agencies must work to prevent illegal tobacco sales to minors, and citizens can pressure them to do so. Retailers, despite operating outside the law by selling unauthorized products, can make the responsible choice not to sell those products to minors, and anyone who knows a retailer is selling to minors should report them to their state’s Alcohol Beverage Control (ABC) agency.

School Interventions

The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) and other federal agencies are recommending schools adopt a Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS), which provides a framework for educators to match their intervention to students’ specific needs:

  • Universal Prevention (Tier 1): Schools implement evidence-based programs like CATCH My Breath or the Truth Initiative’s curriculum. The former is unique in its community and parent involvement, designed to ensure that the vape-free message is unified across home, school, and community.
  • Targeted Interventions (Tier 2): For students at higher risk, schools can implement more focused small-group supports, including interactive digital tools like SmokeSCREEN, a video game that helps students rehearse refusal and navigate peer pressure.
  • Individualized Support (Tier 3): For students dealing with active dependence, school counselors provide one-on-one counseling that focuses on individual risk factors and self-efficacy.

Restorative Accountability

When students are discovered to be vaping, schools must recognize that punishment doesn’t cure addiction. They can choose instead to focus on positive supports, which a modest body of research finds more effective than punitive measures (Cantera-Rios et al., 2024). Restorative programs, such as the American Lung Association’s INDEPTH, serve as alternatives to suspension or detention. INDEPTH provides an educational, community-style setting where students can safely and honestly evaluate their dependence, learn to manage withdrawal symptoms, and build quit-readiness.

Closing Thoughts

The mandate is already clear to many of us working in recovery: We should be treating nicotine dependence with the same seriousness, skill, and compassion we bring to any substance use disorder. The sooner other institutions do the same, the more people we can help quit (or never start).
